Parsing
• Implementation of parsers
• Two approaches
– Top-down
– Bottom-up
• First: Top-Down
– Easier to understand and program manually
• Then: Bottom-Up
– More powerful and used by most parser generators 
1

Top down Parsing
• Top-down parsing is a parsing technique in which we start constructing the parse tree from the root 
node and move towards the leaf nodes. 
• The root represents the start symbol of the grammar. 
• At every step, we select a production rule to expand a non-terminal into terminals and/or other non-
terminals. 
• The parser continues expanding nodes until the generated symbols match the input string. 
• Therefore, the direction of construction is from top to bottom. 
• The nodes of the parse tree are created in preorder—the parent node is processed before its children. 
• Another important way to understand top-down parsing is through derivation. 
• Top-down parsing attempts to find a leftmost derivation of the given input string. 
• In leftmost derivation, the leftmost non-terminal is expanded first at every step. 
• Common top-down parsing techniques include recursive descent parsing and predictive (LL) parsing
2

Example … Parse Tree Construction Steps
1. Start with the root node
• The root is labelled with the start symbol of the grammar (Ex: <S> or <program> or <type>).
2. Repeat two steps until the tree is complete
•
Step 1: Expansion (Which production?)
•
If the current node is a non-terminal (like <expr> or <stmt>), we must choose one of its 
grammar rules (productions).
•
Example: If <expr> → <expr> + <term> | <term>, we must decide which production rule applies.
•
After choosing, expand it by creating child nodes for each symbol in the production.
•
Step 2: Next node (Which node?)
•
After expanding, we look for the next non-terminal node in the tree that still needs to be 
expanded.
•
This continues until all non-terminals are replaced with terminal symbols (tokens from the input 
program).
Decides how to expand a non-terminal.
Decides where to expand next in the tree.

Problem with Expansion
•
The non-terminal simple can never generate a string starting with "array".
•
But our input starts with the token array.
•
This means parsing fails at this stage, and the parser would need backtracking to try other rules.
Back-tracking is not desirable therefore, take help of a “look ahead” token here (array). 
The current token is treated as look-ahead token.

Recursive Descent Parsing → Notes
• Easy to implement by hand
• Somewhat inefficient (due to backtracking)
• But does not always work … 
When Recursive Descent Does Not Work 
This is left-recursive because the non-terminal S 
appears at the leftmost position on the right-hand 
side of its own production.
            S⇒Sa⇒Saa⇒Saaa⇒⋯
11

Why Recursive Descent Fails
• Recursive descent works when the grammar is predictive (LL(1)):
• No left recursion
• No ambiguity
• Parser can decide the production by looking at the next input token (1 lookahead)
Fixing the Grammar (Remove Left Recursion)
12
•
Consider the left-recursive production:  S → Sa | ε. 
•
This causes recursive descent to repeatedly call S() without consuming any input, resulting in infinite recursion. 
Therefore, we need to eliminate left recursion before using recursive descent. 
•
Introduce a new non-terminal S′ and transform the grammar into: 
•
S → ε S′ 
•
S′ → a S′ | ε 
•
Since εS′ is equivalent to S′, this can also be written as: S → S′ and S′ → aS′ | ε. 
•
The new grammar is right-recursive, so the parser can consume a tokens before making further recursive calls. 
•
Therefore, left-recursion elimination makes the grammar suitable for recursive descent/predictive parsing.
